attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post, in his own voice. The adjacent Dietterich quote is separate and is not part of this claim.

semantics.note: The normalised wording keeps the 'isn't magic' antecedent, the 'risk' wording, 'upping', the disclosure caveat and 'many orders of magnitude'. Labelling it a conditional forecast is fair. The harm part is framed as risk, which is possibility language.

contract.note: The contract rightly flags that 'magic' is undefined. It also flags that the claim has no measure of harm, no baseline, no deadline and no probability standard. Any result would depend on evaluator choices the speaker did not supply, so the not_applicable axis is fair.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own GPT-5 launch post (Aug 2025) claims better reliability. This is a company disclosure and cannot settle whether GPT-5 'isn't magic'.

OpenAI's GPT-6 page shows the company was pursuing a GPT-6 family before the evaluation date (Sept 2026 update). That covers only the narrow 'try for GPT-6' part, not the antecedent or the environmental harm.
IEA scenarios cover all data-centre electricity emissions, not AI alone, and they are projections. Different scope and metric, so this cannot contradict an undated warning about risk.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast whose antecedent ('isn't magic') has no criterion, so whether it was met is unknown. Under policy, a conditional is not scored when its antecedent is unknown. The harm part is also hedged as 'risk', has no measure or baseline, and has no deadline. GPT-6 development is shown (e2), but that does not resolve the claim. The IEA data are context only.
